source_batch.unit_label: BRBL Module A unit 4: returns, inspection, winding up, mergers and acquisitions

facts.statement: Annual accounts and balance sheet (courseware): Section 29 of the Banking Regulation Act requires every banking company to prepare its balance sheet and profit and loss account as at the end of each calendar year, or on the expiry of the twelve months ending with any other date the Central Government notifies; foreign banks cover the business transacted through all their branches in India. In preparing accounts banks comply with Reserve Bank directions on income recognition, asset classification and provisioning. The accounts of a banking company incorporated in India are signed by the manager or principal officer and at least three directors (or all if not more than three directors); for foreign banks, by the manager or agent at the principal office in India. The forms are in the Third Schedule, and the Central Government may amend the form after not less than three months notice. The Companies Act 2013 provision on true and fair view and Schedule III formats does not apply to banking companies as the Banking Regulation Act has overriding effect (Section 29(3A) makes certain Companies Act provisions on the profit and loss account period inapplicable). Listed banks publish unaudited quarterly results (clause 41 of the listing agreement as cited). Publication (Section 31 with Rule 15 of the Banking Regulation (Companies) Rules, 1949): the accounts and balance sheet with the auditors report are published in a newspaper circulated at the place of the principal office within six months from the end of the period; newspaper means one published at least once a week but not a journal other than a newspaper. Submission: three copies of the balance sheet, profit and loss account and auditors report to the Reserve Bank within three months of the end of the period, extendable by up to a further three months. For the Registrar of Companies, Section 32 of the Banking Regulation Act requires three copies to the Registrar, dealt with as if submitted under the Companies Act.

Audit and auditors (courseware): Section 30(1) of the Banking Regulation Act requires the balance sheet and profit and loss account prepared under Section 29 to be audited by a person duly qualified under any law for the time being in force to be an auditor of companies. Section 30(1A) requires Reserve Bank approval for the appointment, reappointment or removal of auditors of a banking company. The auditor has the powers, functions and duties of a company auditor and the liabilities and penalties (Section 227 of the Companies Act 1956, Section 143 of the 2013 Act) and in the audit report of a bank incorporated in India must state: whether information and explanations required were found satisfactory; whether transactions are within the powers of the company; whether returns from branches were adequate; whether the profit and loss account shows a true picture of profit or loss; and any other matter the auditor considers necessary to bring to the notice of the shareholders. The auditor of a bank is not restricted to safeguarding promoters but also owes responsibility to depositors, the public and other stakeholders because the bank deals with public money; an auditor can be blamed if after an apparently sound balance sheet is certified the bank is found insolvent (cases cited). The Reserve Bank in 2018 put in place an Enforcement Action Framework in respect of lapses of statutory auditors of commercial banks to ensure quality audits. Special audit (Section 30(1B)): the Reserve Bank may order a special audit of the accounts of any banking company in the public interest or in the interest of the banking company or its depositors, relating to any transaction or class of transactions or any period; the audit may be by the same or a different qualified auditor appointed by the Reserve Bank or by the statutory auditor; the order binds the bank and auditor; the auditor reports to the Reserve Bank with a copy to the bank; and the bank bears the expenses.

Returns (courseware): a banking company submits returns of several kinds. Section 24(3): a return of liquid assets within twenty days of the end of the month, in the form prescribed by Rule 13A of the Banking Regulation (Companies) Rules, 1949, giving assets and demand and time liabilities at the close of business on each alternate Friday; the Reserve Bank may also require a return of assets and liabilities as at each day of the month. Section 27 (monthly returns): each month a return showing assets and liabilities as at the close of business on the last Friday of the previous month, submitted before the close of the following month in the form prescribed by Rule 14A; the Reserve Bank may call for statements and information on business and affairs at any time and may also seek half-yearly returns on investments or classification of advances by industry, commerce or agriculture. Annual accounts and balance sheet: submitted to the Reserve Bank within three months, extendable by a further three months. Section 25(1): a quarterly return on assets in India within one month of the quarter end, in Rule 14A form. Section 26: a return of unclaimed deposits within thirty days of the end of each calendar year, in the form of Rule 14B. Non-scheduled banks: cash reserve return under Section 18 by the twentieth of the month, with the form in Rule 13A. Scheduled banks: returns under Section 42 of the Reserve Bank Act in Form I. A defaulting bank is liable to penal interest at 3 per cent above the bank rate on the shortfall in the cash reserve and 5 per cent above for each subsequent day if the default continues.

Preservation of records and paid instruments (courseware): Section 45Y of the Banking Regulation Act lets the Central Government, after consulting the Reserve Bank, make rules specifying the periods for which a banking company shall preserve its books, accounts and other documents, and shall preserve and keep with itself different instruments paid by it. The rules are the Banking Companies (Period of Preservation of Records) Rules, 1985 and the Co-operative Banks (Period of Preservation of Books) Rules, 1985, which specify different periods for different ledgers and registers; the Reserve Bank in January 2008, relying on the Central Information Commission legal view on the Right to Information Act, advised that banks may follow the existing rules; the Reserve Bank may direct a longer period under Section 35A. Under the Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, banks maintain a record of: all cash transactions of more than Rs 10 lakh or equivalent in foreign currency; a series of connected cash transactions below Rs 10 lakh within a month whose aggregate exceeds Rs 10 lakh; all receipts by non-profit organisations of more than Rs 10 lakh; all transactions where forged or counterfeit currency notes have been used; and all suspicious transactions. Records should allow reconstruction of individual transactions and include the nature of the transaction, the amount and currency, the date and the parties. Banks must keep records of transactions, domestic and foreign, for at least five years from the date of the transaction between the bank and the client, and identification documents for at least five years after the business relationship has ended. Return of paid instruments (Section 45Z): a bank may return paid instruments to customers even before the end of the preservation period, but must not return an instrument without making and keeping a true copy by mechanical or other process; the bank may recover from the customer the cost of making copies; customer includes a Government department and a corporation incorporated by or under any law.

Inspection, scrutiny and government-ordered inspection (courseware): under Section 35(1) the Reserve Bank may at any time inspect any banking company and its books and accounts. The Reserve Bank conducts the Annual Financial Inspection of banking companies; now this consists mainly of assessing all types of risks under risk based supervision through the Supervisory Program for Assessment of Risk and Capital (SPARC), ending with Risk Assessment Reports. The Reserve Bank may also conduct any other inspection, including of bank branches, at any time, and must inspect in compliance with a direction of the Central Government, giving the Central Government a copy of the report; after an inspection the bank is given a copy of the inspection report. During inspection officials of the banking company including directors must produce all books, accounts and documents in their custody and the inspecting officer may examine any director or officer on oath. Inspection at the behest of the Government: a copy of the report is sent to the Government, which may after giving the bank an opportunity to make a representation prohibit it from receiving fresh deposits, cancel or modify an order subject to terms, and may publish the inspection report or any part of it if it thinks fit. Scrutiny (Section 35(1A)): the Reserve Bank may at any time cause a scrutiny of the affairs of a banking company and its books and accounts by officers; unlike inspection, providing a copy of the scrutiny report to the bank is not mandatory, but must be provided if the bank asks for it or if adverse action is contemplated; the Reserve Bank may call for books, accounts, documents, statements and information, and may examine on oath any director or officer.

Board for Financial Supervision (courseware): the Reserve Bank inspects and supervises banks; in 1993 the Department of Banking Supervision was set up and in November 1994 the Board for Financial Supervision (BFS) was set up under Regulation 4 of the Reserve Bank of India (Board for Financial Supervision) Regulations, 1994 to provide integrated supervision of credit institutions including commercial and co-operative banks, all-India financial institutions, local area banks, small finance banks, payment banks, credit information companies, non-banking financial companies and primary dealers. The Department of Banking Supervision was bifurcated into the Department of Banking Supervision and the Department of Non-Banking Supervision in August 1997, and later the Department of Co-operative Banking Supervision was set up. From 1 November 2019 the supervision and inspection functions were integrated into a unified Department of Supervision. From 1 April 2019 Section 45NAA of the Reserve Bank Act lets the Reserve Bank direct a non-banking financial company to furnish information relating to its group companies. Composition: the Governor of the Reserve Bank is the chairman; one of the Deputy Governors (usually the one in charge of supervision) nominated by the Governor is the vice chairman; four directors of the Central Board nominated by the Governor for a specified period are members. A sub-committee of the BFS was constituted in April 2018 under Regulations 11 and 12; it exercises the supervision and inspection powers for payments banks, small finance banks, local area banks, small foreign banks, select urban co-operative banks, select non-banking financial companies and credit information companies, and is chaired by the Deputy Governor in charge of supervision. Functions include: fine tuning the supervisory processes; off-site surveillance; strengthening statutory audit and the role of auditors; strengthening internal defences such as corporate governance, internal control and audit and risk control; a supervisory rating system; supervision of overseas operations of Indian banks and consolidated supervision; technical assistance for co-operative banks; a Prompt Corrective Action framework for weak banks; a fraud risk management framework; risk based supervision; an enforcement framework; a credit registry for large borrowers; and a subsidiary for IT requirements including cyber security. Meetings: normally once every month, with three members, of whom one is the chairman or vice chairman, as the quorum. DAKSH, launched on 6 October 2022, is a web-based workflow application for monitoring compliance by supervised entities.

Acquisition of undertakings (courseware): Section 36AE of the Banking Regulation Act lets the Central Government acquire the undertaking of a banking company, which means its entire organisation (R.C. Cooper v Union of India). Conditions: on receipt of a report from the Reserve Bank the Central Government is satisfied that the banking company (a) has on more than one occasion failed to comply with directions given in writing under Section 21 or 35A relating to banking policy, or (b) is being managed in a manner detrimental to the interests of its depositors, in the interests of banking policy or for the better provision of credit. The Government may, after consultation with the Reserve Bank, acquire the undertaking by a notified order from a specified date (the appointed day), after giving the bank a reasonable opportunity of showing cause. On acquisition all assets and liabilities of the acquired bank vest in the Central Government, which may order vesting in a company or corporation (the transferee bank). Section 36AF: the Central Government makes a scheme for the acquired bank in consultation with the Reserve Bank on property, assets, liabilities, board of management, service of employees and payment of compensation to shareholders; the scheme is placed before Parliament, has overriding effect and binds the acquired bank, its members, creditors and depositors. Section 36AG: shareholders of the acquired bank are entitled to compensation determined in accordance with the principles in the Fifth Schedule; Section 36AH provides for reference to a tribunal if the compensation offered is not acceptable; a foreign bank may request a reference.

Amalgamation and moratorium (courseware): Voluntary amalgamation (Section 44A): a banking company may be amalgamated with another; the scheme is placed before the shareholders of both companies, and must be approved by a resolution passed by a majority in number representing two-thirds in value of the shareholders of each company present in person or by proxy; every shareholder gets notice; a shareholder who votes against or dissents and gives notice may claim the value of his shares from the bank in the event the Reserve Bank sanctions the scheme; after approval the scheme is submitted to the Reserve Bank for sanction; on sanction the assets and liabilities pass to the transferee bank and the Reserve Bank may direct that the amalgamated company stands dissolved. Amalgamation by Government: the Central Government may order the amalgamation of two banking companies under Section 396 of the Companies Act 1956 (Section 237 of the 2013 Act), but only after consulting the Reserve Bank. Moratorium (Section 45): where it appears good reason exists, the Reserve Bank may apply to the Central Government for a moratorium, staying the commencement or continuation of any action or proceedings against the bank for a fixed period on such terms as the Government thinks fit; the period is extendable from time to time but the total period shall not exceed six months; during moratorium the bank shall not make any payment to depositors or discharge liabilities unless the Central Government directs. Scheme: during the moratorium or at any time the Reserve Bank may prepare a scheme for the reconstruction of the banking company or its amalgamation with another bank if necessary in the public interest, in the interests of the depositors, for securing proper management or in the interest of the banking system; the scheme may provide for constitution, name and capital of the reconstructed or transferee bank, transfer of assets, change in the board, alteration of the memorandum, reduction of the interest or rights of members, depositors or creditors, payment in cash, allotment of shares and continuation of service of employees. Employees continue on the same terms; within three years of the scheme employees may opt out. Sanction: a copy of the draft scheme goes to the Government and the banks concerned, which may send suggestions within a period fixed by the Reserve Bank; the Government may sanction the scheme with modifications and it comes into force on the date specified. Effect: the sanction by the Government is conclusive evidence of compliance with Section 45; assets and liabilities vest in the transferee bank; difficulties can be removed by order laid before Parliament; the Central Government may give exemptions for not more than seven years; a single scheme may cover several banks under moratorium; the provisions of Section 45 and the scheme have overriding effect over other laws, agreements, awards or instruments.

Winding up of banks (courseware): winding up of a bank is the process of dissolution when it ceases to do business as usual, to sell off assets, pay creditors and distribute any remaining amount to shareholders; the Banking Regulation Act provides a machinery by which winding up proceedings are expedited. Suspension of business (Section 37): a banking company temporarily unable to meet obligations may apply to the High Court for staying the commencement or continuance of proceedings for a fixed period; the total moratorium shall not exceed six months; the application must be supported by a report of the Reserve Bank that the bank will be able to pay its debts if the application is allowed; if the Reserve Bank is satisfied that the bank is being conducted detrimentally to the interests of depositors it may apply to the High Court for winding up. Winding up by the High Court (Section 38): the High Court shall order winding up if the bank is unable to pay its debts or an application has been made by the Reserve Bank under Section 37 or Section 38; the Reserve Bank is bound to apply if directed by the Central Government under Section 35(4) after an inspection or scrutiny at its direction; and the Reserve Bank may apply where the bank fails to comply with Section 11 on minimum paid-up capital and reserves, is not entitled to carry on banking under Section 22 by rejection or cancellation of licence, is prohibited from accepting fresh deposits under Section 35(4) or Section 42(3A) of the Reserve Bank Act, fails to comply with requirements under Section 11 beyond the period specified, or in the opinion of the Reserve Bank a compromise or arrangement cannot be worked, the returns show it cannot pay its debts or its continuance is prejudicial to the interests of the depositors. A bank is deemed unable to pay its debts if it has refused to meet any lawful demand made at any of its offices or branches within the stipulated time and the Reserve Bank certifies in writing that the bank is unable to pay its debts: two days where the Reserve Bank has an office, branch or agency, otherwise five days. In the Palai Central Bank case the Supreme Court held that the decision to wind up in the interests of depositors is reasonably left to the Reserve Bank. Court liquidator (Section 38A): attached to every High Court, appointed by the Central Government, to conduct winding up of banking companies, though the Central Government may notify that a High Court need not have one. Official liquidator (Section 39): the Reserve Bank, the State Bank or another bank notified, or an individual named in the application, may be appointed official liquidator by the High Court on the Reserve Bank application. The liquidator makes a preliminary report within two months of the winding up order on the availability of assets for preferential payments and discharge of liabilities and gives notice calling for claims within fifteen days. Depositors need not make claims (Section 43): the claim of each depositor is deemed filed for the amount in the books of the bank. Preferential payment (Section 43A): the liquidator makes certain preferential payments first, in addition to Section 327 of the Companies Act, to depositors in savings accounts up to a limit; the balance goes to general creditors and then to further amounts due to depositors; the provision does not apply to deposits covered by deposit insurance. Voluntary winding up (Section 44): permitted only if the Reserve Bank certifies that the bank will be able to pay all its debts in full as they accrue; the High Court may order winding up by the court, during voluntary winding up, if it becomes clear that the bank cannot meet its debts or voluntary winding up is detrimental to the interests of depositors.

Penalties (courseware): a banking company must abide by the Reserve Bank Act, the Banking Regulation Act and the rules, directions and regulations under them; non-compliance invites penalties. Reserve Bank Act, Chapter V: false statements in an application, return or statement, known to be false or wilfully omitting a material statement, are punishable with imprisonment up to three years and also a fine; failure to produce books or documents is punishable with a fine and, for continuing offences, a daily fine; Sections 58B(3) to 58B(5B) deal with contravention of Chapter IIIB directions including Sections 31, 45E and 45J. Offences by companies: every person in charge of and responsible for the conduct of the business is deemed guilty unless proved the offence was committed without knowledge or with due diligence; a court takes cognizance of an offence under the Act (other than Chapter IIIC deposit offences) only on a complaint by an officer of the bank generally or specially authorised in writing; a metropolitan magistrate or a first class judicial magistrate tries the offences. Banking Regulation Act: Section 46 deals with penalties for false statements, failure to produce documents or information, contravention of Section 35(4)(a) (deposits taken in contravention of an order, punishable with fine up to twice the deposits taken) and other contraventions or defaults with fine and, for continuing contravention, a further daily fine; Section 47: cognizance only by a metropolitan magistrate or judicial magistrate of the first class (or superior) on a complaint of an officer of the Reserve Bank (and in some cases the National Bank); Section 47A: the Reserve Bank may itself impose a penalty for default or contravention; if it exercises this power, no complaint is filed in court for the same contravention or default.

payload.title: Annual accounts and the balance sheet (Section 29)
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Preparation (Section 29):** every banking company prepares its **balance sheet and profit and loss account** at the **end of each calendar year**, or at the end of **twelve months ending on another date the Central Government notifies**. **Foreign banks** cover business through **all branches in India**. Banks follow **Reserve Bank directions** on **income recognition, asset classification and provisioning**.

**Signature:** by the **manager or principal officer** and **at least three directors** (all directors if there are three or fewer); for a foreign bank, by the **manager or agent** at the principal office in India.

**Form:** the **Third Schedule**, which the Government may amend after **three months' notice**. The **Banking Regulation Act overrides** the Companies Act on the form and the true-and-fair-view requirement.

**Publication (Section 31):** with the auditor's report, in a **newspaper circulating at the place of the principal office**, **within six months** of the period end.

**To the Reserve Bank:** **three copies within three months** of the period end, **extendable by a further three months**. **To the Registrar of Companies:** **three copies** (Section 32).
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Act gives banks their own accounting framework because the Reserve Bank needs the accounts in a uniform form.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many months of the end of the period must a bank submit three copies of its accounts to the Reserve Bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Within three months, extendable by a further three months.

payload.title: Audit and auditors (Section 30) and special audit
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Audit (Section 30(1)):** by a person **qualified to be a company auditor**. **Section 30(1A):** **Reserve Bank approval** is needed to **appoint, re-appoint or remove** the auditor.

**Duties:** the auditor has the **Companies Act** powers and liabilities and reports on the **adequacy of information and explanations**, whether transactions are **within the company's powers**, whether **branch returns** were adequate, whether the **profit and loss account is true**, and any matter for the **shareholders' attention**.

**Wider responsibility:** the auditor owes duties to **depositors and the public** because the bank deals in **public money**. The **2018 Enforcement Action Framework** deals with lapses by statutory auditors of commercial banks.

**Special audit (Section 30(1B)):** the Reserve Bank may order it **in the public interest** or in the interest of the **bank or its depositors**, for any **transaction, class of transactions or period**; the auditor may be **a different qualified auditor appointed by the Reserve Bank** or the **statutory auditor**; the order **binds the bank and the auditor**; the **report goes to the Reserve Bank** with a copy to the bank; the **bank pays**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A special audit gives the regulator an independent look at a specific problem without waiting for the annual audit.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the expenses of a special audit ordered by the Reserve Bank under Section 30(1B)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The banking company.

payload.title: Returns to the Reserve Bank
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Return | Provision | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Liquid assets** | **Section 24(3)** (Rule 13A) | **Within 20 days** of the month end, with positions on each **alternate Friday** |
| **Monthly return of assets and liabilities** | **Section 27** (Rule 14A) | **Before the close of the next month**, showing the **last Friday** position |
| **Assets in India** | **Section 25(1)** (Rule 14A) | **Within one month** of the **quarter end** |
| **Unclaimed deposits** | **Section 26** (Rule 14B) | **Within 30 days** of the **calendar year end** |
| **Accounts and balance sheet** | **Section 29** | **Within three months**, extendable by **three more** |
| **Non-scheduled banks: cash reserve** | **Section 18** (Rule 13A) | **By the 20th of the month** |
| **Scheduled banks** | **Section 42, RBI Act** (**Form I**) | Alternate Fridays |

The Reserve Bank may also call for **any statement or information** at any time, **returns for each day** of a month, and **half-yearly** returns on **investments** and **advances by sector**.

**Penalty for a cash reserve default:** **3 per cent above the bank rate** on the shortfall and **5 per cent above** if it continues.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Returns give the regulator a regular view of liquidity and asset positions across the banking system.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many days of the end of the month must the return of liquid assets be submitted under Section 24(3)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Within twenty days.

payload.title: Preservation of records and return of paid instruments
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Section 45Y:** the Central Government, after consulting the Reserve Bank, makes **rules on how long a bank keeps its books, accounts, documents and paid instruments**. The rules are the **Banking Companies (Period of Preservation of Records) Rules, 1985** and the **Co-operative Banks** equivalent; the Reserve Bank may direct **longer periods** under **Section 35A**.

**Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005:** a bank keeps a record of all **cash transactions above Rs 10 lakh**; **connected cash transactions** below Rs 10 lakh whose **monthly total exceeds Rs 10 lakh**; **non-profit organisation receipts above Rs 10 lakh**; transactions with **forged or counterfeit notes**; and all **suspicious transactions**. The record must allow **reconstruction of a transaction**: **nature, amount and currency, date and parties**. Transaction records are kept for **at least five years** from the transaction, and **identification documents for at least five years** after the relationship ends.

**Return of paid instruments (Section 45Z):** a bank may **return a paid instrument** to the customer before the preservation period ends, but only after **making and keeping a true copy** (mechanical or other process); it may **recover the copying cost**. **Customer** includes a **Government department** and a **statutory corporation**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A true copy lets the bank return the original to the customer without losing the evidence of the transaction.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long must a bank keep records of transactions under the PML Maintenance of Records Rules as the courseware states them?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least five years from the date of the transaction.

payload.title: Inspection and scrutiny (Section 35)
payload.core_explanation_md:
- **Inspection (Section 35(1)):** the Reserve Bank may inspect a bank **at any time**; the **Annual Financial Inspection** is now mainly a **risk based supervision** exercise (**SPARC**) producing a **Risk Assessment Report**. A **copy of the inspection report goes to the bank**.
- **Duties during inspection:** directors and officials must **produce all books, accounts and documents**; the inspecting officer may **examine any director or officer on oath**.
- **Inspection on Government direction:** the Reserve Bank **must inspect** and give the Government a copy; the Government may, after the bank has had an **opportunity to represent**, **prohibit fresh deposits**, **cancel or modify** an order subject to terms, and **publish** the report.
- **Scrutiny (Section 35(1A)):** by **officers at any time**; a **copy of the scrutiny report is not mandatory**, but must be given **if the bank asks** or if **adverse action** against the bank is contemplated.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Scrutiny is the lighter, quicker tool; inspection is the full examination with a report the bank must receive.

self_check.prompt_text: Is the Reserve Bank bound to give the bank a copy of a scrutiny report in all cases?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it must give a copy if the bank asks for it or if adverse action is contemplated.

payload.title: The Board for Financial Supervision
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Origin:** the **Department of Banking Supervision** (1993) and the **Board for Financial Supervision (BFS)** in **November 1994**, under the **Reserve Bank of India (Board for Financial Supervision) Regulations, 1994**; **supervision of non-banking finance companies** moved to a separate department in **1997**; a **unified Department of Supervision** from **1 November 2019**.

**Composition:** the **Governor** (chairman); **one Deputy Governor**, usually the one in charge of supervision (vice chairman); **four directors of the Central Board** nominated by the Governor.

**Sub-committee (April 2018):** chaired by the **Deputy Governor in charge of supervision**; handles **small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, small foreign banks, selected urban co-operative banks, and selected NBFCs and credit information companies**.

**Functions:** **off-site surveillance**, **supervisory rating**, **Prompt Corrective Action** for weak banks, **fraud risk management**, **risk based supervision**, an **enforcement framework**, a **credit registry for large borrowers**, and strengthening **audit and internal controls**.

**Meetings:** normally **monthly**; **three members** (including the chairman or vice chairman) form the **quorum**. **DAKSH** (6 October 2022) is a web-based **compliance monitoring workflow**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The BFS joins bank and non-bank supervision under one authority within the Reserve Bank.

self_check.prompt_text: Who chairs the Board for Financial Supervision?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Governor of the Reserve Bank of India.

payload.title: Acquisition of the undertaking of a banking company
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Section 36AE:** the Central Government may **acquire the undertaking** (the **entire organisation**) of a banking company after a **Reserve Bank report**, if the bank:

- has **more than once failed to comply with written directions** under **Section 21 or 35A** on **banking policy**; or
- is **managed detrimentally** to **depositors**, **banking policy** or the **better provision of credit**.

The Government acts **after consulting the Reserve Bank**, by a **notified order** from an **appointed day**, after giving the bank a **reasonable opportunity to show cause**.

**Effect:** all **assets and liabilities vest in the Central Government**, which may vest them in a **company or corporation** (the **transferee bank**).

**Section 36AF:** a **scheme** (property, assets, liabilities, board, employees, **compensation to shareholders**) made **with the Reserve Bank**, laid before **Parliament**, with **overriding effect**.

**Section 36AG:** shareholders get **compensation** under the **Fifth Schedule**; **Section 36AH:** a **tribunal reference** is available if the offer is not acceptable.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Acquisition is the strongest step short of winding up, used when a bank defies policy directions or is badly managed.

self_check.prompt_text: Whose report must the Central Government have before acquiring the undertaking of a banking company under Section 36AE?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Reserve Bank.

payload.title: Amalgamation, moratorium and schemes of reconstruction
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Voluntary amalgamation (Section 44A):** the scheme goes to the **shareholders of both banks**; it needs a **majority in number representing two-thirds in value** of shareholders **present in person or by proxy**; a **dissenting shareholder** who gives notice may claim **the value of his shares**; the scheme then needs **Reserve Bank sanction**.

**Amalgamation by Government:** under **Section 396 of the Companies Act 1956 (Section 237 of the 2013 Act)**, **after consulting the Reserve Bank**.

**Moratorium (Section 45):** on the Reserve Bank's application the **Central Government** may stay actions and proceedings against a bank for a **fixed period, extendable, total not more than six months**; during it the bank **makes no payments to depositors** unless the Government directs.

**Scheme of reconstruction or amalgamation:** the Reserve Bank may prepare it **during or after** the moratorium **in public interest, depositors' interest, for proper management or for the banking system**. It may deal with **capital, assets and liabilities, board, memorandum, reduction of rights of members, depositors and creditors, payment and employees**. **Employees continue** on the same terms (with an **option to leave within three years**).

**Sanction and effect:** the **Central Government sanctions** the scheme after **suggestions and objections** from the banks concerned; the sanction is **conclusive evidence** of compliance; the scheme has **overriding effect**; **exemptions** can last **up to seven years**; **one scheme** can cover **several banks** under moratorium.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: A moratorium buys time while the Reserve Bank designs a rescue by reconstruction or merger.

self_check.prompt_text: What shareholder majority is needed for a voluntary amalgamation under Section 44A?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A majority in number representing two-thirds in value of those present in person or by proxy, in each company.

payload.title: Winding up of banking companies
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Suspension (Section 37):** a bank temporarily unable to pay may apply to the **High Court** to stay proceedings for a **fixed period, total not more than six months**, supported by a **Reserve Bank report** that it will be able to pay.

**Winding up by the High Court (Section 38):** **mandatory** if the bank is **unable to pay its debts** or the **Reserve Bank applies**. The Reserve Bank **must apply** if the **Central Government directs** (Section 35(4)). It **may apply** if the bank **fails Section 11 capital requirements**, **loses its licence**, is **barred from taking deposits**, a **compromise cannot work**, the **returns show it cannot pay**, or its **continuance prejudices depositors**.

**Deemed inability to pay:** a refused **lawful demand** plus a **Reserve Bank certificate**; the demand must be met within **two days** at a place where the Reserve Bank has an office or branch, and within **five days elsewhere**. The courts leave the decision to wind up to the Reserve Bank (**Palai Central Bank**).

**Liquidators:** each High Court has a **court liquidator** (**Section 38A**); the **official liquidator (Section 39)** may be the Reserve Bank, the State Bank or another notified bank. The liquidator reports within **two months** and invites claims within **15 days**.

**Depositors:** claims are **deemed filed** from the bank's books (**Section 43**); **preferential payment** to savings depositors up to a limit (**Section 43A**), not covered by deposit insurance.

**Voluntary winding up (Section 44):** only if the **Reserve Bank certifies** the bank can **pay all debts in full**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The winding up rules favour speed and depositor protection, and let the Reserve Bank, not creditors, trigger the process.

payload.core_explanation_md:
**RBI Act, Chapter V:** **false statements** in an application, return or statement (or wilful omission of a material fact) carry **imprisonment up to three years and a fine**; **failure to produce documents** carries a **fine**, with a **daily fine** for continuing offences. **Sections 58B(3) to 58B(5B)** cover contraventions of the **Chapter IIIB** directions.

**Companies:** **every person in charge and responsible** for the conduct of business is **deemed guilty** unless he shows the offence occurred **without his knowledge** or that he used **due diligence**. A court takes cognisance only on a **complaint by an authorised Reserve Bank officer** (except **Chapter IIIC deposit offences**); a **metropolitan magistrate or first class judicial magistrate** tries them.

**Banking Regulation Act:** **Section 46** penalises **false statements**, **failure to produce information**, **taking deposits against an order under Section 35(4)(a)** (a **fine up to twice the deposits taken**) and **other contraventions** with **fines and daily fines**. **Section 47:** cognisance only on a complaint by the Reserve Bank (or **NABARD** in some cases). **Section 47A:** the Reserve Bank may **impose a penalty itself**; if it does, **no complaint is filed in court** for the same default.

items.title: Annual accounts and the balance sheet (Section 29)
items.core_explanation_md:
**Preparation (Section 29):** every banking company prepares its **balance sheet and profit and loss account** at the **end of each calendar year**, or at the end of **twelve months ending on another date the Central Government notifies**. **Foreign banks** cover business through **all branches in India**. Banks follow **Reserve Bank directions** on **income recognition, asset classification and provisioning**.

**Signature:** by the **manager or principal officer** and **at least three directors** (all directors if there are three or fewer); for a foreign bank, by the **manager or agent** at the principal office in India.

**Form:** the **Third Schedule**, which the Government may amend after **three months' notice**. The **Banking Regulation Act overrides** the Companies Act on the form and the true-and-fair-view requirement.

**Publication (Section 31):** with the auditor's report, in a **newspaper circulating at the place of the principal office**, **within six months** of the period end.

**To the Reserve Bank:** **three copies within three months** of the period end, **extendable by a further three months**. **To the Registrar of Companies:** **three copies** (Section 32).
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Act gives banks their own accounting framework because the Reserve Bank needs the accounts in a uniform form.

self_check.prompt_text: Within how many months of the end of the period must a bank submit three copies of its accounts to the Reserve Bank?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Within three months, extendable by a further three months.

items.title: Audit and auditors (Section 30) and special audit
items.core_explanation_md:
**Audit (Section 30(1)):** by a person **qualified to be a company auditor**. **Section 30(1A):** **Reserve Bank approval** is needed to **appoint, re-appoint or remove** the auditor.

**Duties:** the auditor has the **Companies Act** powers and liabilities and reports on the **adequacy of information and explanations**, whether transactions are **within the company's powers**, whether **branch returns** were adequate, whether the **profit and loss account is true**, and any matter for the **shareholders' attention**.

**Wider responsibility:** the auditor owes duties to **depositors and the public** because the bank deals in **public money**. The **2018 Enforcement Action Framework** deals with lapses by statutory auditors of commercial banks.

**Special audit (Section 30(1B)):** the Reserve Bank may order it **in the public interest** or in the interest of the **bank or its depositors**, for any **transaction, class of transactions or period**; the auditor may be **a different qualified auditor appointed by the Reserve Bank** or the **statutory auditor**; the order **binds the bank and the auditor**; the **report goes to the Reserve Bank** with a copy to the bank; the **bank pays**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A special audit gives the regulator an independent look at a specific problem without waiting for the annual audit.

self_check.prompt_text: Who bears the expenses of a special audit ordered by the Reserve Bank under Section 30(1B)?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The banking company.

items.title: Returns to the Reserve Bank
items.core_explanation_md:
| Return | Provision | Timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Liquid assets** | **Section 24(3)** (Rule 13A) | **Within 20 days** of the month end, with positions on each **alternate Friday** |
| **Monthly return of assets and liabilities** | **Section 27** (Rule 14A) | **Before the close of the next month**, showing the **last Friday** position |
| **Assets in India** | **Section 25(1)** (Rule 14A) | **Within one month** of the **quarter end** |
| **Unclaimed deposits** | **Section 26** (Rule 14B) | **Within 30 days** of the **calendar year end** |
| **Accounts and balance sheet** | **Section 29** | **Within three months**, extendable by **three more** |
| **Non-scheduled banks: cash reserve** | **Section 18** (Rule 13A) | **By the 20th of the month** |
| **Scheduled banks** | **Section 42, RBI Act** (**Form I**) | Alternate Fridays |

The Reserve Bank may also call for **any statement or information** at any time, **returns for each day** of a month, and **half-yearly** returns on **investments** and **advances by sector**.

**Penalty for a cash reserve default:** **3 per cent above the bank rate** on the shortfall and **5 per cent above** if it continues.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Returns give the regulator a regular view of liquidity and asset positions across the banking system.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Within twenty days.

items.title: Preservation of records and return of paid instruments
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 45Y:** the Central Government, after consulting the Reserve Bank, makes **rules on how long a bank keeps its books, accounts, documents and paid instruments**. The rules are the **Banking Companies (Period of Preservation of Records) Rules, 1985** and the **Co-operative Banks** equivalent; the Reserve Bank may direct **longer periods** under **Section 35A**.

**Prevention of Money Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005:** a bank keeps a record of all **cash transactions above Rs 10 lakh**; **connected cash transactions** below Rs 10 lakh whose **monthly total exceeds Rs 10 lakh**; **non-profit organisation receipts above Rs 10 lakh**; transactions with **forged or counterfeit notes**; and all **suspicious transactions**. The record must allow **reconstruction of a transaction**: **nature, amount and currency, date and parties**. Transaction records are kept for **at least five years** from the transaction, and **identification documents for at least five years** after the relationship ends.

**Return of paid instruments (Section 45Z):** a bank may **return a paid instrument** to the customer before the preservation period ends, but only after **making and keeping a true copy** (mechanical or other process); it may **recover the copying cost**. **Customer** includes a **Government department** and a **statutory corporation**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A true copy lets the bank return the original to the customer without losing the evidence of the transaction.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long must a bank keep records of transactions under the PML Maintenance of Records Rules as the courseware states them?
self_check.expected_takeaway: At least five years from the date of the transaction.

items.title: Inspection and scrutiny (Section 35)
items.core_explanation_md:
- **Inspection (Section 35(1)):** the Reserve Bank may inspect a bank **at any time**; the **Annual Financial Inspection** is now mainly a **risk based supervision** exercise (**SPARC**) producing a **Risk Assessment Report**. A **copy of the inspection report goes to the bank**.
- **Duties during inspection:** directors and officials must **produce all books, accounts and documents**; the inspecting officer may **examine any director or officer on oath**.
- **Inspection on Government direction:** the Reserve Bank **must inspect** and give the Government a copy; the Government may, after the bank has had an **opportunity to represent**, **prohibit fresh deposits**, **cancel or modify** an order subject to terms, and **publish** the report.
- **Scrutiny (Section 35(1A)):** by **officers at any time**; a **copy of the scrutiny report is not mandatory**, but must be given **if the bank asks** or if **adverse action** against the bank is contemplated.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Scrutiny is the lighter, quicker tool; inspection is the full examination with a report the bank must receive.

self_check.prompt_text: Is the Reserve Bank bound to give the bank a copy of a scrutiny report in all cases?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No; it must give a copy if the bank asks for it or if adverse action is contemplated.

items.title: The Board for Financial Supervision
items.core_explanation_md:
**Origin:** the **Department of Banking Supervision** (1993) and the **Board for Financial Supervision (BFS)** in **November 1994**, under the **Reserve Bank of India (Board for Financial Supervision) Regulations, 1994**; **supervision of non-banking finance companies** moved to a separate department in **1997**; a **unified Department of Supervision** from **1 November 2019**.

**Composition:** the **Governor** (chairman); **one Deputy Governor**, usually the one in charge of supervision (vice chairman); **four directors of the Central Board** nominated by the Governor.

**Sub-committee (April 2018):** chaired by the **Deputy Governor in charge of supervision**; handles **small finance banks, payments banks, local area banks, small foreign banks, selected urban co-operative banks, and selected NBFCs and credit information companies**.

**Functions:** **off-site surveillance**, **supervisory rating**, **Prompt Corrective Action** for weak banks, **fraud risk management**, **risk based supervision**, an **enforcement framework**, a **credit registry for large borrowers**, and strengthening **audit and internal controls**.

**Meetings:** normally **monthly**; **three members** (including the chairman or vice chairman) form the **quorum**. **DAKSH** (6 October 2022) is a web-based **compliance monitoring workflow**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The BFS joins bank and non-bank supervision under one authority within the Reserve Bank.

self_check.prompt_text: Who chairs the Board for Financial Supervision?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Governor of the Reserve Bank of India.

items.title: Acquisition of the undertaking of a banking company
items.core_explanation_md:
**Section 36AE:** the Central Government may **acquire the undertaking** (the **entire organisation**) of a banking company after a **Reserve Bank report**, if the bank:

- has **more than once failed to comply with written directions** under **Section 21 or 35A** on **banking policy**; or
- is **managed detrimentally** to **depositors**, **banking policy** or the **better provision of credit**.

The Government acts **after consulting the Reserve Bank**, by a **notified order** from an **appointed day**, after giving the bank a **reasonable opportunity to show cause**.

**Effect:** all **assets and liabilities vest in the Central Government**, which may vest them in a **company or corporation** (the **transferee bank**).

**Section 36AF:** a **scheme** (property, assets, liabilities, board, employees, **compensation to shareholders**) made **with the Reserve Bank**, laid before **Parliament**, with **overriding effect**.

**Section 36AG:** shareholders get **compensation** under the **Fifth Schedule**; **Section 36AH:** a **tribunal reference** is available if the offer is not acceptable.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Acquisition is the strongest step short of winding up, used when a bank defies policy directions or is badly managed.

self_check.prompt_text: Whose report must the Central Government have before acquiring the undertaking of a banking company under Section 36AE?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Reserve Bank.

items.title: Amalgamation, moratorium and schemes of reconstruction
items.core_explanation_md:
**Voluntary amalgamation (Section 44A):** the scheme goes to the **shareholders of both banks**; it needs a **majority in number representing two-thirds in value** of shareholders **present in person or by proxy**; a **dissenting shareholder** who gives notice may claim **the value of his shares**; the scheme then needs **Reserve Bank sanction**.

**Amalgamation by Government:** under **Section 396 of the Companies Act 1956 (Section 237 of the 2013 Act)**, **after consulting the Reserve Bank**.

**Moratorium (Section 45):** on the Reserve Bank's application the **Central Government** may stay actions and proceedings against a bank for a **fixed period, extendable, total not more than six months**; during it the bank **makes no payments to depositors** unless the Government directs.

**Scheme of reconstruction or amalgamation:** the Reserve Bank may prepare it **during or after** the moratorium **in public interest, depositors' interest, for proper management or for the banking system**. It may deal with **capital, assets and liabilities, board, memorandum, reduction of rights of members, depositors and creditors, payment and employees**. **Employees continue** on the same terms (with an **option to leave within three years**).

**Sanction and effect:** the **Central Government sanctions** the scheme after **suggestions and objections** from the banks concerned; the sanction is **conclusive evidence** of compliance; the scheme has **overriding effect**; **exemptions** can last **up to seven years**; **one scheme** can cover **several banks** under moratorium.
items.expanded_explanation_md: A moratorium buys time while the Reserve Bank designs a rescue by reconstruction or merger.

self_check.prompt_text: What shareholder majority is needed for a voluntary amalgamation under Section 44A?
self_check.expected_takeaway: A majority in number representing two-thirds in value of those present in person or by proxy, in each company.

items.title: Winding up of banking companies
items.core_explanation_md:
**Suspension (Section 37):** a bank temporarily unable to pay may apply to the **High Court** to stay proceedings for a **fixed period, total not more than six months**, supported by a **Reserve Bank report** that it will be able to pay.

**Winding up by the High Court (Section 38):** **mandatory** if the bank is **unable to pay its debts** or the **Reserve Bank applies**. The Reserve Bank **must apply** if the **Central Government directs** (Section 35(4)). It **may apply** if the bank **fails Section 11 capital requirements**, **loses its licence**, is **barred from taking deposits**, a **compromise cannot work**, the **returns show it cannot pay**, or its **continuance prejudices depositors**.

**Deemed inability to pay:** a refused **lawful demand** plus a **Reserve Bank certificate**; the demand must be met within **two days** at a place where the Reserve Bank has an office or branch, and within **five days elsewhere**. The courts leave the decision to wind up to the Reserve Bank (**Palai Central Bank**).

**Liquidators:** each High Court has a **court liquidator** (**Section 38A**); the **official liquidator (Section 39)** may be the Reserve Bank, the State Bank or another notified bank. The liquidator reports within **two months** and invites claims within **15 days**.

**Depositors:** claims are **deemed filed** from the bank's books (**Section 43**); **preferential payment** to savings depositors up to a limit (**Section 43A**), not covered by deposit insurance.

**Voluntary winding up (Section 44):** only if the **Reserve Bank certifies** the bank can **pay all debts in full**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The winding up rules favour speed and depositor protection, and let the Reserve Bank, not creditors, trigger the process.

self_check.prompt_text: For how long can a High Court stay proceedings against a bank under Section 37 at most?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Six months in total.

items.title: Penalties for contravention
items.core_explanation_md:
**RBI Act, Chapter V:** **false statements** in an application, return or statement (or wilful omission of a material fact) carry **imprisonment up to three years and a fine**; **failure to produce documents** carries a **fine**, with a **daily fine** for continuing offences. **Sections 58B(3) to 58B(5B)** cover contraventions of the **Chapter IIIB** directions.

**Companies:** **every person in charge and responsible** for the conduct of business is **deemed guilty** unless he shows the offence occurred **without his knowledge** or that he used **due diligence**. A court takes cognisance only on a **complaint by an authorised Reserve Bank officer** (except **Chapter IIIC deposit offences**); a **metropolitan magistrate or first class judicial magistrate** tries them.

**Banking Regulation Act:** **Section 46** penalises **false statements**, **failure to produce information**, **taking deposits against an order under Section 35(4)(a)** (a **fine up to twice the deposits taken**) and **other contraventions** with **fines and daily fines**. **Section 47:** cognisance only on a complaint by the Reserve Bank (or **NABARD** in some cases). **Section 47A:** the Reserve Bank may **impose a penalty itself**; if it does, **no complaint is filed in court** for the same default.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The Reserve Bank can either prosecute through the courts or impose a penalty itself, but not both for the same default.

self_check.expected_takeaway: No; only on a complaint by an authorised Reserve Bank officer (or NABARD in some cases).
